part_title: Reinforcement Learning Applications and Safe Sequential Decisions
review_basis: Original numbered AIF Module 03 WebP slides 37–37 visually inspected in sequence; image titles, examples, numbers and diagrams take priority over legacy lesson map.

scenes.title: Applications of Reinforcement Learning
scenes.narration: This slide applies the agent, action, reward and policy concepts we have learned to actual problems. Start with the robot on the far left. An agent is a decision-making system that observes a situation, chooses an action, receives feedback and uses experience to improve its policy. A policy is the strategy for choosing actions. Follow the row of five application panels. In gaming, an agent can practice moves against opponents and learn strategies that yield better outcomes over many turns; the chess board is an example, not a promise of perfect play. In robotics, a mechanical arm may practice picking up and placing objects in a changing environment, where success, efficiency and safety matter. The finance panel illustrates trading or portfolio strategies, but real markets have uncertainty and learning a profitable strategy from past prices does not guarantee returns. The healthcare panel suggests optimizing treatment decisions from observed results, yet real medical decisions must involve rigorous evidence, clinical safety and human oversight. The autonomous driving panel shows a vehicle navigating traffic. Here exploration directly on public roads would be hazardous, so simulation, safety constraints and formal testing are essential. Now move to the lower left four-step driving example. First the car observes the road, other vehicles and signals. Second it chooses an action, such as slowing down or changing lanes. Third it receives feedback related to progress, safety and rule-following. Finally, it improves decisions over many experiences. This diagram is conceptual; not every autonomous driving product uses reinforcement learning in the same way. The bottom right gives the key choice: consider reinforcement learning when actions affect later states and the goal involves long-term consequences rather than a single isolated classification. A quick test: if we merely need to label a photo as car or bicycle, would reinforcement learning usually be the first choice? No; supervised image classification may fit better. If a simulated robot must choose a sequence of safe moves to reach a destination, reinforcement learning becomes more relevant.
